posts.title: UK settlement now takes 10 years for most people: what Nigerians on work visas should know
posts.excerpt: The Home Office has confirmed that the standard wait for Indefinite Leave to Remain will double from five to ten years. Here's who is affected, who gets a faster route, and what to do now.
posts.content:
Quick gist: On 2 November 2026 the UK government confirmed its "earned settlement" plan. For most migrants, the wait for permanent residence (ILR) moves from 5 years to 10. A few groups get faster routes. The rules haven't been laid in Parliament yet, so nothing has changed in law today, but the direction is now clear.

If you came to the UK on a Skilled Worker or Health and Care visa thinking "five years and I'm settled", this is the news you've been dreading. Let's break it down without the panic.

What exactly was announced?

The Home Secretary set out the final shape of the new system in Parliament on 2 November. In the government's own words, the right to stay forever "will no longer be granted to migrants almost automatically after 5 years". The new default is 10 years for people who are working, paying in and following the rules.

There are faster and slower lanes:

  • Faster: the highest earners can settle in as little as 3 years. People earning above about £50,000, some public service workers, relatives of British citizens and Hong Kong BN(O) holders keep a 5-year route.
  • Default: 10 years for most workers.
  • Slower: people who have breached immigration rules or entered illegally face much longer waits, 20 years or more.

The new must-haves for everyone

According to the Migration Observatory's breakdown, every settlement applicant will need to tick these boxes:

  1. English at B2 level, up from B1.
  2. No debts owed to the government and a clean record. That now includes cautions and court fines.
  3. Pass the Life in the UK test, as before.
  4. Minimum earnings of around £12,571 a year for several years. Couples can meet this jointly.

That English requirement is the one to start working on now. B2 is upper-intermediate. Many Nigerians will pass it comfortably, but get your certificate sorted early so it isn't a last-minute scramble.

I'm already in the UK on a 5-year route. Am I affected?

This is the big question, and the honest answer is: mostly yes, with some protections. The government has said no one will be forced to leave. One protection that has been confirmed is for care workers who arrived before 12 May 2025: they can still settle after 5 years if their employer followed the rules and paid at least £25,000.

What you should know:

  • Don't switch visas without advice. Under the new plans, the qualifying period has to be completed on your current route, so switching can restart your clock.
  • Partners and children settle with you if they came with you. Children aged 18–24 who are still your dependants can settle alongside you too.
  • Watch the dates. Legal firms tracking the plan say the rule changes are due to start being laid from December 2026 and roll out through 2027. Until they're in the Immigration Rules, the current 5-year rules still apply.

What to do this week

  • Count your days. Work out exactly when you'd hit 5 years under today's rules. If it's close, talk to a regulated adviser (OISC-registered or a solicitor) about whether you can apply before the changes start.
  • Book your English test if you don't already have B2 or a UK degree that counts.
  • Keep your record spotless. Pay any council tax arrears, parking fines or HMRC debts. Small debts can now cost you years.
  • Keep payslips and P60s. You'll need to show earnings over several years.

The bigger picture

The Home Office's own figures suggest about 500,000 people who would have settled between 2026 and 2030 will now wait longer. That's a lot of families. Expect immigration advisers to be very busy over the coming months, so if you need help, book early.

We'll keep updating this as the actual rules are published. Subscribe to the GistDew Daily email so you don't miss it.

This is general information, not legal advice. Your situation may be different, so check with a regulated immigration adviser.

posts.title: Wizkid wins International Male Artist at Brazil's 2026 BreakTudo Awards, beating Burna Boy and Bieber
posts.excerpt: Big Wiz did it again. Wizkid has won International Male Artist at the BreakTudo Awards in São Paulo, his second win in the category.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Wizkid has won International Male Artist at the 2026 BreakTudo Awards, held in São Paulo, Brazil, on 24 November 2026. He beat a big list that included Burna Boy, Bad Bunny, Bruno Mars, Harry Styles, Justin Bieber, Sombr and The Weeknd. It's his second win in the category after 2023.

Starboy FC, you can come out now. 🙌🏾

The win

The BreakTudo Awards were set up in 2016 and celebrate music, TV and internet culture. Winners are decided by fan votes, which says a lot about how hard Wizkid's fanbase mobilised.

The nominees for International Male Artist were:

  • Wizkid (winner)
  • Burna Boy
  • Bad Bunny
  • Bruno Mars
  • Harry Styles
  • Justin Bieber
  • Sombr
  • The Weeknd

That is not a soft category. Two Nigerians on a list with some of the biggest names in global pop shows how far Afrobeats has travelled.

Wizkid vs Burna Boy: round who-knows-what

Of course, the timeline immediately turned into another Wizkid vs Burna Boy argument. Wizkid fans are calling it proof of his global pull. Burna fans are quick to point out that it's a fan-voted award, so it measures who mobilised the most votes.

Our take? Two Nigerian artists competing for a Brazilian award against Bieber and The Weeknd is a win for everyone in the culture. But you can still tell us in the comments who you think deserved it. 😄

Why Brazil loves Afrobeats

Brazil has one of the world's largest populations of African descent, and Afrobeats has been growing there for years through streaming, TikTok and collaborations with Brazilian artists. Wins like this help Nigerian artists book more shows in Latin America, which is a big and growing touring market.

What's next for Big Wiz?

Wizkid is also expected to headline the opening night of the Detty December Fest in Lagos on 18 December, with general access tickets reported from ₦50,000. If you're flying home for Christmas, that could be one way to celebrate the win in person.

Have your say: who's the bigger global star right now, Wizkid or Burna? Drop your vote in the comments.

posts.title: Pound to naira this week: official vs black market, and when to send money home
posts.excerpt: The pound is trading around ₦1,820 officially and ₦1,850–₦1,900 on the parallel market this week. Here's what that means for your next transfer home.
posts.content:
Quick gist: On 26 November 2026, the pound was around ₦1,821 at the CBN official rate and roughly ₦1,850–₦1,900 on the parallel market, depending on which tracker you check. The dollar was around ₦1,390 officially. The gap between official and street rates is now small, so you rarely need the black market to get good value.

Rates move every day, so treat these as a snapshot. Here's how to read them and get the most naira for your pounds.

This week's numbers (26 November 2026)

CBN official Parallel (sell)
£1 (GBP) about ₦1,821 ₦1,850–₦1,909
$1 (USD) about ₦1,392 ₦1,390–₦1,460
€1 (EUR) about ₦1,525 about ₦1,560
CA$1 (CAD) about ₦990 about ₦986

Sources: Abokiforex, NairaToday and NGNRates, 24–26 November 2026. Parallel rates vary by city and dealer.

Mid-month, the official rate ranged from about ₦1,780 to ₦1,808 per pound. The naira has been fairly stable this month, which is good news for families planning December budgets.

Official vs parallel: does it still matter?

A few years ago the gap was huge and many people went through informal channels. Today the difference is only a few percent. And since May 2026, CBN rules require licensed money transfer companies to pay out in naira, priced at market rates.

That means a good transfer app usually gets you close to the street rate, with:

  • no cash-handling risk
  • a proper record of the transfer, which matters if you ever need to show source of funds
  • no risk of being caught up in a fraud investigation with an unknown dealer

How to get the most naira for your pounds

  1. Compare the final amount received, not just the rate. Some apps advertise a great rate and hide a fee. Others charge no fee but use a weaker rate.
  2. Check two or three apps before every big transfer. Rates change daily and the best app this week might not be the best next week.
  3. Send larger amounts less often. Fixed fees hurt small transfers most.
  4. Avoid sending on weekends if you can. Some providers widen their margins when markets are closed.
  5. Watch for promotions. Many apps give better rates on your first transfer, so new users can save a little.

Sending for December?

December demand usually pushes rates around and fills family WhatsApp groups with requests. If you know what you'll send for the festive season, consider sending in early December rather than the week before Christmas.

Exchange rates are for information only and change constantly. GistDew isn't a financial adviser. Check the live rate with your provider before sending.

posts.title: Detty December 2026: the Lagos shows, ticket prices and what it really costs to go home
posts.excerpt: Wizkid, Davido, Asake, Lauryn Hill and more. Here are the Detty December 2026 dates and prices so far, plus the flight costs nobody warns you about.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Detty December 2026 is shaping up big: Wizkid opens Detty December Fest on 18 Dec, Davido has a residency at the National Theatre on 17–19 Dec, Asake headlines on 20 Dec, and Lauryn Hill plays with YG and Zion Marley on 21 Dec. General tickets start from about ₦25,000–₦100,000. Flights are the real cost: London–Lagos returns in mid-December are being quoted from roughly £1,200 to £1,600.

If you're japa-ing back for the holidays, here's your planner.

The big shows (dates and starting prices)

Detty December Fest, Detty December Village, Lagos (18–28 Dec) - 18 Dec — Wizkid opening concert: from ₦50,000 (golden circle reported at ₦150,000, VIP standing ₦300,000) - 21 Dec — Lauryn Hill with YG Marley and Zion Marley: from ₦50,000 - 24 Dec — DJ Tunez & Friends Christmas Eve special: from ₦25,000 - 25 Dec — Tungba Christmas: from ₦35,000 - 27 Dec — Summer Walker and Fridayy: from ₦50,000 - 28 Dec — Young Thug: from ₦50,000

Davido: ORIADÉ The Residency, National Theatre, Iganmu (17–19 Dec) - Seats listed from ₦80,000, with tiers up to about ₦2 million

Future Fest, Oasis Ground, Victoria Island - 18 Dec — YBNL: The Reunion (Olamide, Adekunle Gold, Fireboy DML and others): price not yet published - 20 Dec — Asake's M$NEY in Lagos: general from ₦100,000, VIP ₦250,000, VVIP ₦300,000, and a platinum table at… ₦20 million 👀

Still to be priced: Flytime Fest (22–24 Dec, with Latto, A Boogie Wit da Hoodie and Sexyy Red on opening night), Rhythm Unplugged (21 Dec), Brandy's House of R&B (20 Dec), ICONIQ Fest at Lekki Coliseum (19–23 Dec, with BNXN, FOLA, Oxlade, Ruger and Mr P), and Adekunle Gold's The Greatest Showman with the MUSON Orchestra (26 Dec).

Prices are from published reports and ticketing pages as of mid-November and may change. Always buy from official ticket platforms.

The flight shock

The concert ticket is often the cheap part.

  • London → Lagos: airline sites were quoting mid-December returns from about £1,200 to over £1,600 on some dates. Early-December departures were cheaper, around £700–£1,000.
  • Domestic flights: a THEWILL check found Lagos and Abuja to South-East and South-South economy fares of ₦196,000–₦337,500 for 20–21 December. One Lagos–Asaba fare jumped about 208% compared with early November.

Money-saving tips: 1. Fly out early December and return early January if your job allows. The 18–24 December window is the most expensive. 2. Book domestic legs now. Prices only climb as Christmas gets closer. 3. Set a budget per event and stick to it. Detty December has broken many bank accounts. 😅 4. Keep valuables light at big shows and use official transport options.

Are you going?

Tell us which show you're buying tickets for, and if you're flying in from the UK, US or Canada, which airline gave you the best deal.

posts.title: AFCON 2027 qualifiers: can the Super Eagles still qualify? Where things stand
posts.excerpt: A 3-1 win over Tanzania was followed by a frustrating 0-0 draw, and Guinea-Bissau have moved three points clear. Only one of the two can go to AFCON 2027.
posts.content:
Quick gist: After beating Tanzania 3-1 in Uyo, the Super Eagles were held 0-0 in Zanzibar. Nigeria have 7 points from four games. Group leaders Guinea-Bissau then beat Madagascar 2-0 to move on to 10 points. Because Tanzania qualify automatically as co-hosts, only one more team from Group L goes to AFCON 2027, so it's effectively Nigeria vs Guinea-Bissau.

Another qualifying campaign, another set of nerves. Here's where things stand.

How we got here

  • Matchday 1: Nigeria 2-1 Madagascar (Uyo)
  • Matchday 2: lost 3-0 to Guinea-Bissau. Ouch.
  • Matchday 3: Nigeria 3-1 Tanzania (Uyo). Tolu Arokodare came off the bench and scored twice in eight minutes.
  • Matchday 4: Tanzania 0-0 Nigeria (Zanzibar). Coach Eric Chelle made seven changes, and the reshuffled team couldn't break Tanzania down.

Why Tanzania's result matters less than you'd think

AFCON 2027 will be hosted by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania from 19 June to 17 July 2027. As co-hosts, Tanzania already have a place. That means Group L's other qualifying spot goes to the highest-placed team among Nigeria, Guinea-Bissau and Madagascar.

Guinea-Bissau beat Madagascar 2-0 in the same round we drew, which puts them three points clear. That 3-0 defeat on matchday 2 could come back to haunt us, because it also gives them the edge if it comes down to head-to-head.

What Nigeria need

  • Win the remaining games. No more slip-ups against Madagascar.
  • Beat Guinea-Bissau in Bissau. That return fixture is effectively a final, and pundits are already backing the Eagles to do it.
  • Hope Guinea-Bissau drop points elsewhere.

It's no longer fully in our hands. Nigeria need wins and some help, with no room left for mistakes.

The pressure on Chelle

Pundits, including former Super Eagles coach Jo Bonfrere, have warned that Nigeria must improve or risk missing AFCON 2027. After also missing the 2026 World Cup, missing AFCON would be a disaster for the NFF and for Chelle.

Questions remain about team selection, the goalkeeper position and why the team looks so different from one match to the next.

Diaspora fans

If you're watching from the UK or US, most AFCON qualifiers stream through broadcasters with African football rights or official CAF channels, depending on where you are. Check listings closer to matchday.

Who should start up front in the decider? Osimhen, Arokodare or someone else? Let us know.

posts.title: UK Graduate visa: two years for "high-compliance" universities, 18 months for everyone else
posts.excerpt: The 2026 Budget partly reversed the Graduate visa cut. If you're finishing a UK degree, the date you apply could decide whether you get 18 months or two years.
posts.content:
Quick gist: From 1 January 2027 the standard UK Graduate visa drops from 2 years to 18 months. But the UK Budget on 28 October 2026 said graduates of "high-compliance universities with strong labour market outcomes" will keep 2 years. The list of universities hasn't been published yet. If you can apply on or before 31 December 2026, you still get the full 2 years.

Nigerians are among the biggest users of the Graduate route. Vanguard reported that Nigerian nationals received over 20,000 Graduate route approvals in the period it reviewed, making them the third-largest group. So this one affects a lot of us.

What changed, step by step

  1. Earlier this year the government announced that the Graduate visa for bachelor's and master's graduates would fall from 2 years to 18 months for applications from 1 January 2027.
  2. On 28 October 2026 the Budget softened that. It said the visa "will be set at two years for individuals who graduate from high-compliance universities where there are strong labour market outcomes".
  3. PhD graduates still get 3 years either way.

So in 2027 there will effectively be two tiers: 2 years for some universities and 18 months for the rest.

Which universities count as "high-compliance"?

Nobody knows yet. The government hasn't published the list or the exact test. "High compliance" usually refers to how well a university does on Home Office checks, such as visa refusal rates and how many students complete their courses. "Strong labour market outcomes" suggests graduate earnings and job data will matter too.

Until the list is out, don't assume your university is on it.

What it means for you

If you finish your course this year: you need to be in the UK on your Student visa and your university must have reported your successful completion. If you can apply on or before 31 December 2026, you get 2 years under the current rules. Don't sit on it.

If you finish in 2027: you'll get 18 months unless your university makes the high-compliance list. Plan your job search for the shorter window. That gives you less time to find a Skilled Worker sponsor.

If you're choosing a university now: once the list is published, it becomes a real factor. An extra 6 months of work rights can be the difference between finding a sponsor and going home.

Quick tips to make the most of your Graduate visa

  • Start job hunting in your final term, not after graduation.
  • Target employers who already hold a sponsor licence. The UK government publishes the full register of licensed sponsors.
  • Keep the fee ready. The Graduate visa application fee plus the Immigration Health Surcharge for the full period adds up to a few thousand pounds.

You can work out your exact cost on our sister site, VisaCost Hub.

General information, not legal advice. Check GOV.UK for the official position before you apply.

posts.title: AMAA 2026: Wale Ojo and Linda Ejiofor lead Nigeria's eight wins in Lagos
posts.excerpt: Nigerian films picked up eight awards at the 22nd Africa Movie Academy Awards, with Wale Ojo winning Best Actor and Linda Ejiofor taking Best Supporting Actress.
posts.content:
Quick gist: The 22nd Africa Movie Academy Awards took place on Sunday 15 November 2026 at the Marriott Hotel, Ikeja, Lagos. Nigeria won eight awards. Wale Ojo won Best Actor in a Leading Role for Lights Out, and Linda Ejiofor won Best Actress in a Supporting Role for The Herd. The Kenya–Nigeria co-production One Woman, One Bra took Best Film.

Nollywood's finest dressed up, showed up and took home some serious hardware. Here's what you need to know.

The big winners

  • Best Film: One Woman, One Bra (Kenya/Nigeria). It also won Best Debut Feature Film.
  • Best Actor in a Leading Role: Wale Ojo, Lights Out (Nigeria)
  • Best Actress in a Leading Role: Naky Sy Savane, The Color of Exile (Côte d'Ivoire)
  • Best Actress in a Supporting Role: Linda Ejiofor, The Herd (Nigeria)

The Color of Exile from Côte d'Ivoire led the night with four trophies, and Kenyan cinema also had a big showing. It was a reminder that the African film scene is much bigger than Nollywood alone.

The Herd keeps winning

Daniel Etim-Effiong's The Herd was one of Nigeria's standout films of the night. Beyond Linda Ejiofor's acting win, it also took Achievement in Production Design and Achievement in Make-up. Etim-Effiong was also nominated for Best Actor.

Linda Ejiofor's incredible year

This caps a huge 2026 for Linda Ejiofor. Back in May, she became the first actress to win both Best Lead and Best Supporting Actress at the AMVCAs on the same night. Adding an AMAA to that makes her one of the most decorated Nollywood actresses of the year.

Wale Ojo: still got it

Wale Ojo has been a Nollywood heavyweight for years, and Lights Out has now earned him one of the continent's top acting awards. He was also nominated at the AMVCAs in May for 3 Cold Dishes, so it's been a strong year for him too.

Where to watch

Many AMAA winners do a festival run before landing on streaming. Keep an eye on Netflix, Prime Video and the newer African platforms over the coming months for The Herd, Lights Out and One Woman, One Bra.

Which winner made you happiest? Tell us in the comments.

posts.title: CBN remittance rules explained: why your family now gets naira, and what changed for crypto
posts.excerpt: Since May 2026, money sent home through transfer companies is paid out in naira. In November the CBN also brought crypto remittances under the same rules. Here's what it means for you.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Since 1 May 2026, licensed money transfer operators (IMTOs) such as the big transfer apps must route remittances through naira settlement accounts at Nigerian banks and price them at live market rates. Your family receives naira, not dollars. In November 2026, the CBN said crypto sent home as a personal remittance must also go through a licensed operator, with the receiver paid in naira.

If you've noticed that your mum can no longer receive dollars through your usual app, this is why.

The May 2026 rules in plain English

The CBN issued a circular on 24 March 2026, which took effect on 1 May 2026. The key points:

  • Naira settlement accounts: every licensed transfer company must process payouts through designated naira accounts at authorised Nigerian banks.
  • Market pricing: transfer companies must set their rates using live market prices rather than rates they pick themselves.
  • Stricter monitoring: every transaction is more traceable, as part of the CBN's push to bring diaspora money into the formal system.

What it means for you as a sender

  • Your family gets naira. If they relied on receiving dollars to save in dollars, that route through transfer apps has largely closed.
  • Rates should be fairer and more transparent. Because transfer companies have to price close to the market, the gap between app rates and street rates has narrowed.
  • More checks. Expect identity checks and occasional questions about large or frequent transfers. That's normal, not a sign you've done anything wrong.

What changed for crypto in November

Many Nigerians abroad started sending USDT or USDC home to get around naira payouts. On 5 November 2026 the CBN issued new regulations covering virtual assets. A payout guide published on 13 November says an inbound personal remittance using crypto may now only be handled by a licensed IMTO, or a licensee working with one, and the person receiving it is paid in naira.

In short, sending crypto peer-to-peer as a "remittance" now sits in a grey area. If you send crypto home, understand that the rules have tightened and your recipient could face questions from their bank.

Practical tips

  1. Use licensed providers. It protects you and your family.
  2. Keep records of what you send and why: school fees, upkeep, building. It helps if a bank ever asks.
  3. Paying school fees abroad for a sibling? The CBN raised the tuition remittance cap to $25,000 per semester, but that is for payments out of Nigeria through banks, a different channel.
  4. Want to save in dollars for family? Talk to a Nigerian bank about domiciliary account options, which are separate from transfer-app payouts.

GistDew provides general information, not financial or legal advice. Rules change, so check with your bank or provider.

posts.title: UK student visa: proof of funds goes up from 30 November — the new amounts
posts.excerpt: Applying for a UK Student visa for the January 2027 intake? From 30 November you'll need to show more money for living costs. Here are the new figures.
posts.content:
Quick gist: For UK Student visa applications made on or after 30 November 2026, the monthly living-cost amount rises to £1,570 in London and £1,203 outside London. You show up to 9 months, so that's up to £14,130 in London or £10,827 elsewhere, plus any unpaid first-year tuition.

If you're targeting the January 2027 intake, this lands right in the middle of your application season. Here's what you need to know.

The new amounts

The change comes from the Home Office's Statement of Changes HC 584, laid before Parliament on 3 September 2026.

Before 30 Nov 2026 From 30 Nov 2026
London (per month) £1,529 £1,570
Outside London (per month) £1,171 £1,203
London, 9 months £13,761 £14,130
Outside London, 9 months £10,539 £10,827

The rise is about £300–£370 over 9 months. That's not huge in pounds, but at today's exchange rate it's roughly half a million naira or more extra to keep in your account.

What doesn't change

  • The 28-day rule: the full amount must sit in your account for 28 consecutive days, ending no more than 31 days before you apply.
  • The visa fee and the Immigration Health Surcharge aren't part of this change.
  • Applications submitted before 30 November are assessed on the old amounts.

Apply before or after?

If your CAS is ready, your money has already been sitting for 28 days and you can submit before 30 November, you'll be assessed at the lower rate. But don't rush a sloppy application to save a few hundred pounds. A refusal costs far more.

If you're applying after 30 November, top up your balance before your 28-day period starts. The amount must be in your account for the whole 28 days. You can't add the extra halfway through.

Naira savers: watch the exchange rate

If your funds are in naira, the Home Office converts them using the OANDA rate on the day you apply, not the day you deposit. If the naira weakens during your 28 days, you could fall short. A 5–10% buffer is a sensible safety margin.

Work it out in seconds

Our free calculator at VisaCost Hub switches to the new rates automatically for applications on or after 30 November. It shows the total in naira or cedis and gives you a dated 28-day plan.

General information only. Always confirm the current figures on GOV.UK before you apply.

posts.title: Canada's 2027–2029 immigration plan: Express Entry cut, provinces get more spots
posts.excerpt: Canada will keep 380,000 new permanent residents a year, but Express Entry loses places to the provinces. Here's what that means if you're planning a Canada move.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Canada released its 2027–2029 Immigration Levels Plan on 5 November 2026. It keeps 380,000 new permanent residents a year, but the federal Express Entry target falls to 100,000 and provincial programmes rise to 95,000. There's also a one-off measure for up to 200,000 people already in Canada. On 25 November, MPs voted down an attempt to reject the plan, so it stands.

For Nigerians eyeing Canada, the message is simple: the provinces matter more than ever.

The headline numbers

  • 380,000 permanent residents a year from 2027 to 2029.
  • 370,000 new temporary residents (workers and students) a year.
  • Express Entry (Federal High Skilled): 100,000 in 2027, down from a planned 111,000.
  • Provincial Nominee Program (PNP): 95,000, up.
  • Up to 200,000 extra PR spaces in 2027 through a time-limited measure for people already living in Canada, including up to 45,000 spaces for spouses, partners and children of Canadians and permanent residents.

What it means if you're still in Nigeria

Express Entry is still the main door for skilled workers abroad, but it's getting narrower. Recent draws have favoured people with Canadian work experience, provincial nominations and French skills. A high score from abroad alone is getting harder to rely on.

Practical moves:

  1. Look seriously at provincial programmes. Many provinces run streams for in-demand jobs such as healthcare, trades and tech, and some accept people who are outside Canada.
  2. Consider French. French-language draws have been among the biggest this year. Even moderate French can add a lot of points.
  3. Max out your English score. Every point on IELTS or CELPIP counts.

What's happening with Express Entry draws?

On 3 November 2026, new Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) rules took effect, including a new "labour market integration" factor and the return of points for job offers without an LMIA. IRCC paused invitation rounds while it recalculated every profile in the pool. The last round before the pause was on 28 October. Check IRCC's rounds page for the latest draw, because cut-off scores may move once rounds settle under the new rules.

Already in Canada on a work or study permit?

The 200,000 extra spaces for 2027 are aimed at you. Details are being released group by group. IRCC published the breakdown for spouses and dependants on 10–12 November. Keep your documents current and watch for the stream that fits you.

Bottom line

Canada isn't closing its doors, but it's choosing more carefully. If you're serious, build a plan B around a specific province.

General information, not legal advice. Use a licensed RCIC for your own case.

posts.title: New Nollywood this November: Loving Itohan, Dear Ajayi, Issakaba returns and The Covenant season 2
posts.excerpt: Five Nigerian films hit cinemas this month and The Covenant is back on Netflix. Here's what to watch, whether you're in Lagos or London.
posts.content:
Quick gist: November 2026 is a busy month for Nollywood. Loving Itohan (6 Nov), Dear Ajayi, Issakaba: The Return and Five Figurines (13 Nov) and Ray of Hope (20 Nov) are all in Nigerian cinemas, and The Covenant season 2 has arrived on Netflix.

Whether you're home or watching from abroad, here's the guide.

In Nigerian cinemas

Loving Itohan (from 6 November, FilmOne) Nancy Isime and Uzor Arukwe lead a romantic drama about Itohan, her childhood love and the experiences that shape her. Expect big chemistry and big emotions.

Dear Ajayi (wide release from 13 November, FilmOne) Set in 1990s south-west Nigeria, two estranged sisters are forced to live together again to care for their paralysed mother. With Bimbo Akintola and Tosin Adeyemi. It had a limited run from September and is now everywhere.

Issakaba: The Return (13 November, Blue Pictures) Yes, that Issakaba. Twenty-five years after the original vigilante classic, the story returns in present-day Nigeria with Sam Dede, Chidi Mokeme, Iyabo Ojo, Regina Daniels and Nosa Rex. Nostalgia is guaranteed.

Five Figurines (13 November, Cinemax) A heavyweight cast: Bimbo Akintola, Ini Edo, Odunlade Adekola, Ireti Doyle and Uche Montana. Plot details are being kept quiet.

Ray of Hope (20 November, Cinemax) A drama set in the fashion world, with Jide Kene Achufusi, Stan Nze, Bucci Franklin, Uzor Arukwe, Zack Orji and Sunshine Rosman.

On Netflix (watch anywhere)

The Covenant, season 2 The series is back, with a new storyline set in South Africa. Season 1 starred Gideon Okeke, Zubby Michael, Uzee Usman and Sola Sobowale. Reports gave slightly different release dates in early November, so search for it on Netflix in your region.

Watching from abroad?

Most cinema releases make their way to streaming within a few months. If you're in the UK, some Nollywood titles also get screenings at diaspora film nights and selected cinemas, so follow the films' social pages for UK dates.

Our pick

If you only watch one: Dear Ajayi for the drama, or Issakaba: The Return if you grew up on the original and want to see how it's aged.

Seen any of these? Rate them out of 10 in the comments.

posts.title: How to set up your UK eVisa: a simple step-by-step guide
posts.excerpt: BRP cards are gone and the eVisa is now your proof of status in the UK. Here's how to create your UKVI account, prove your identity and link your eVisa without stress.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Your UK immigration status now lives online as an eVisa. To see it and share it with employers, landlords or airlines, you need a UKVI account linked to your eVisa. It takes three steps: create the account, confirm your identity with the "UK Immigration: ID Check" app, and link your eVisa. UKVI has been reminding people of the process again this month.

If you've been putting this off, today's the day. Without access to your eVisa you can have trouble at the airport, with a new job or with a new tenancy.

Do you already have a UKVI account?

Check before you create a new one. You already have one if:

  • you used the UK Immigration: ID Check app when you applied for your visa, or
  • you got a "UKVI account confirmation" email when you applied, or
  • you applied to the EU Settlement Scheme.

If any of those apply, sign in instead. Never create a second account. It causes problems that take weeks to untangle.

What you'll need

  • Your passport or your BRP (an expired BRP can be used for up to 24 months after its expiry date, or until 31 December 2026, whichever comes first)
  • An email address and phone number you'll keep long term
  • A smartphone for the ID Check app. You can borrow a friend's phone for this step, and the app can be deleted afterwards.
  • Ideally a laptop or tablet as well, because you'll switch between the website and the app

Step 1: Create your UKVI account

Go to gov.uk/get-access-evisa and choose to create an account. Enter your details exactly as they appear on your identity document, and check the date format carefully before you submit. You'll get a confirmation email.

Step 2: Confirm your identity

You'll be asked to download the UK Immigration: ID Check app. Use it to:

  1. Scan your passport or BRP. Use the same document you chose when creating the account.
  2. Scan the chip in your document by holding your phone against it.
  3. Take a selfie. Treat it like a passport photo: plain background, no smile, no glasses.

If the app won't read your document, try another phone or take the case off. If you created the account with an old passport, you may need to add your new passport first.

Step 3: Link your eVisa

Follow the on-screen steps to link your account to your eVisa. You'll be asked a few security questions. You'll get an email once it's linked. Sign in and check every detail: your name, date of birth, visa type and expiry date.

Families: everyone needs their own account

Each dependant, including your spouse and every child, needs their own UKVI account and eVisa link. Parents can set these up for children.

Before you travel

  • Make sure your current passport is linked to your UKVI account. If you renewed your Nigerian passport, add the new one before you fly.
  • Generate a share code if an employer or landlord asks for proof of status. Share codes expire, so create a fresh one each time.

Stuck?

GOV.UK has short help videos for every scenario, including what to do if you have no identity document at all. There's also a UKVI Resolution Centre phone line if you can't complete the steps online.

This guide is general information. Always follow the latest instructions on GOV.UK.

posts.title: UK revokes two Global Talent visas over faked evidence — a warning for anyone tempted by "agents"
posts.excerpt: A BBC investigation led the Home Office to cancel two Nigerians' Global Talent visas after their evidence was found to be fabricated. Here's why fake documents always catch up with you.
posts.content:
Quick gist: The UK has revoked the Global Talent visas of two Nigerian men after a BBC investigation found they had used fabricated press reviews to pose as fine-art photographers. The deception came to light when the art critic Molara Wood found reviews published under her name that she never wrote.

This story spread fast in Nigerian WhatsApp groups. Beyond the gossip, there's a serious lesson in it for anyone planning to japa.

What happened

The Global Talent visa is meant for leaders and rising stars in fields such as arts, science and tech. You don't need a job offer, but you do need a strong body of evidence: recognition, reviews, awards and endorsements.

According to reports by TheCable and Legit.ng, the two men presented themselves as photographers with a track record of reviewed work. Molara Wood, an art critic, discovered articles attributed to her that she had never written. She also described the "reviews" and the artworks as poor quality. A BBC investigation followed, and the Home Office moved to revoke the visas.

Why fake documents always come back to bite

Getting the visa isn't the end of the checking. The Home Office can revoke a visa at any point if it finds it was obtained by deception. Once that happens:

  • You can be removed from the UK.
  • You can face a ban on re-entry for up to 10 years.
  • Future applications to the UK, and often to Canada, the US and Australia, will ask whether you've ever been refused or used deception. Lying on those forms makes it worse.
  • Under the new settlement plans, any immigration breach adds years to your path to ILR.

And the people who sold you the "package" are nowhere to be found when it all falls apart.

How to spot a dodgy japa agent

  • They guarantee a visa. Nobody can.
  • They offer to "arrange" documents such as bank statements, job letters, reviews, references or certificates.
  • They ask you to pay big sums in cash or to personal accounts.
  • They won't put anything in writing.
  • In the UK, they aren't registered. Anyone giving UK immigration advice must be regulated by the IAA (formerly OISC) or be a solicitor. You can check the official register online.

The honest route is slower but safer

If Global Talent is your dream, build real evidence. Exhibit, publish, enter competitions and get genuine endorsements. It may take a year or two longer, but a visa you earned can't be taken from you.

GistDew is reporting what was published by the outlets linked below. The men named in the original reports have not commented publicly.

posts.title: Your first UK winter: a survival guide for new arrivals from Nigeria
posts.excerpt: Nobody prepares you for 4pm darkness and a heating bill. Here's how to stay warm, healthy and sane through your first British winter.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Dress in layers, keep at least one room properly warm, take vitamin D from October to March as the NHS suggests, deal with damp early, get a proper coat and boots, and plan for the darkness. Your first winter is the hardest. After that, you'll know the drill.

You've seen the memes. Then the clocks go back, it's pitch dark at 4:30pm, the wind is coming at you sideways and Lagos traffic suddenly seems romantic. Welcome to your first British winter. Here's how to handle it.

1. Layers beat one big jumper

The trick is layers: a thin thermal base layer, a regular top, a jumper or fleece and a proper waterproof coat. Then add gloves, a scarf and a hat. You lose a lot of heat through your head and hands, and no one will laugh at your beanie.

Shoes matter. Canvas sneakers and wet pavements don't mix. Get waterproof boots with a decent grip, because ice is no joke.

2. Heating: warm one room well

Energy bills are a real worry. A few tips:

  • Heat the rooms you use, and close doors to keep the heat in.
  • The NHS suggests keeping the rooms you use regularly at 18°C or higher, especially if you have health conditions or young children.
  • Draught-proof windows and doors with cheap stick-on strips.
  • Thick curtains closed at dusk make a big difference.
  • Hot water bottles and electric blankets are cheap to run compared with heating the whole house.

If you're struggling to pay, contact your energy supplier early. Ofgem has guidance on help schemes, and suppliers have to work with you.

3. Damp and mould: deal with it early

Cold weather plus drying clothes indoors often means condensation, which leads to black mould. To prevent it:

  • Open windows briefly each day, even when it's cold.
  • Use extractor fans when cooking and showering.
  • Wipe condensation off windows in the morning.
  • If you're renting and mould keeps coming back, report it to your landlord in writing. Landlords have legal duties on damp and mould.

4. Vitamin D: the one nobody tells you about

With less sunlight, the NHS advises everyone to consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement from October to March. People with darker skin may not make enough vitamin D from sunlight even in summer, so the NHS suggests some may need it all year. Supermarket brands are cheap.

5. The darkness is real

Short days hit mood hard, especially when you're far from family. What helps:

  • Get outside in daylight, even for a 20-minute lunchtime walk.
  • Plan things to look forward to: church, community events, Naija parties, Sunday rice. 😄
  • Call home on video, not just voice notes.
  • If you feel persistently low, talk to your GP. Low mood in winter is common and treatable, and it's nothing to be ashamed of.

6. Get registered with a GP now

Flu season peaks in winter. Register with a local GP surgery as soon as you can. Ask whether you're eligible for a free flu jab, as some groups are.

7. Plan your travel around the weather

Trains get delayed, buses get cancelled and snow can shut things down. Check travel apps before you leave, and give yourself extra time for work or school.

You'll be fine

By your second winter, you'll be the one sending this to the new arrivals. Stay warm. 🧣

General information only, not medical advice. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about your own health.

posts.title: Where to find Nigerian food in the UK: a beginner's guide for new japa people
posts.excerpt: Craving egusi, ponmo or proper Nigerian rice? Here's where to find Naija ingredients in the UK, what to swap when you can't, and how to save money doing it.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Most UK towns with a sizeable African community have at least one African or "world foods" shop. Big supermarkets now stock plantain, yam, scotch bonnets and some African brands. Online African grocers deliver nationwide. And be careful what you pack from home: the UK has strict rules on bringing in meat and dairy.

The first few weeks abroad, you'll eat a lot of sandwiches and pretend you're fine. Then one day you'll be craving pepper soup so much it hurts. Here's how to find home on a plate.

1. African and Caribbean shops

Search "African shop near me" or "African food store" on Google Maps. Most cities, and many big towns, have at least one. They usually stock:

  • Grains and flours: garri, semovita, poundo, amala flour, beans (oloyin, brown, black-eyed)
  • Soup ingredients: egusi, ogbono, crayfish, dried fish, stockfish, uziza, ugu (sometimes frozen), bitter leaf
  • Proteins: ponmo, goat meat, snails (seasonal), frozen fish
  • Snacks and drinks: chin chin, plantain chips, Malt and Nigerian biscuits

Tip: prices vary a lot between shops, so compare. And ask the shop owner; they often know the community WhatsApp groups and events.

2. Supermarkets are catching up

Big chains in diverse areas now carry:

  • Plantain (ripe and unripe), yam and sweet potatoes
  • Scotch bonnet peppers, which are perfect for your pepper mix
  • Long grain parboiled rice for jollof
  • A "world foods" aisle with some West African brands, seasonings and palm oil

Discount supermarkets can be great for onions, tomatoes and chicken, the backbone of most Naija stews.

3. Online African grocers

If there's no shop nearby, there are many UK-based online African grocers that deliver nationwide. Order in bulk with friends or church members to split delivery costs.

4. Smart swaps when you can't find something

  • Ugu (pumpkin leaf): frozen ugu, or spinach as a backup
  • Bitter leaf: dried or frozen bitter leaf travels well
  • Fresh pepper mix: blend scotch bonnets, tatashe (red bell peppers), tomatoes and onions, then freeze in portions
  • Locust beans (iru): dried or frozen iru is usually available in African shops

5. Be careful what you bring from Nigeria

It's tempting to fill your suitcase with dried fish and meat. But the UK has strict rules on bringing in meat, dairy and some other animal products from outside the EU. Items can be seized at the border, and you can be fined. Many dried plant items such as spices, grains and dried leaves are generally fine. Check the GOV.UK page on bringing food into Great Britain before you travel.

6. Nigerian restaurants and buka spots

London, Manchester, Birmingham and other big cities have Nigerian restaurants, from casual buka-style spots to fancier places. They're great for a taste of home and for meeting other Nigerians. Check Google reviews and community recommendations.

Save money: cook in batches

Cook a big pot of stew on Sunday, portion it out and freeze it. It's cheaper, healthier and it beats queuing for overpriced takeaway jollof. 😉

Where's your favourite African shop or Naija restaurant in the UK? Share it in the comments to help a new arrival.

posts.title: Building a UK credit score from zero: a guide for new arrivals
posts.excerpt: Your Nigerian credit history doesn't follow you to the UK. Here's how to build a UK credit file from scratch so you can rent, get a phone contract and eventually a mortgage.
posts.content:
Quick gist: You arrive in the UK with no credit file. Build one by opening a UK bank account, getting on the electoral register if you're eligible, using a credit-builder card for small purchases and paying it off in full every month, putting bills in your name and avoiding lots of applications in a short time. It takes about 6–12 months to see real progress.

In Nigeria, you might have been doing well, with a car loan paid off and a good relationship with your bank. In the UK, none of that counts. To the UK credit agencies, you're a blank page. Here's how to fill it.

Why it matters

Your credit file affects whether you can get:

  • a phone contract rather than pay-as-you-go
  • a rental flat without a huge deposit or guarantor
  • a car on finance
  • eventually, a mortgage

The UK has three main credit reference agencies: Experian, Equifax and TransUnion. Each keeps its own file on you, and lenders may check any of them.

Step 1: Open a UK bank account

A current account is the foundation. Many digital banks let you open one with just your passport and visa, sometimes before you have proof of address. Use it for your salary and regular spending.

Step 2: Get on the electoral register (if you can)

Being on the electoral roll at your address is one of the easiest ways to show lenders who you are and where you live. Commonwealth citizens, which includes Nigerians, with permission to be in the UK can usually register to vote. Check your eligibility on GOV.UK. It's free and takes minutes.

Step 3: Use a credit-builder card the right way

Credit-builder cards have low limits and higher interest. That's fine, because you're never going to pay interest:

  1. Use it for one small regular purchase, such as a phone top-up or a weekly shop.
  2. Set up a direct debit to pay the full balance every month.
  3. Keep your balance well below the limit. Many lenders like to see usage under about 30%.

Do this for six months and your file starts to look healthy.

Step 4: Put bills in your name

Council tax, energy, broadband and your phone contract all help show you're a reliable payer. Some services also let you add rent payments to your credit file.

Step 5: Avoid these mistakes

  • Don't apply for lots of credit at once. Each full application leaves a "hard search" on your file. Use eligibility checkers, which do soft searches, first.
  • Never miss a payment. One missed payment can stay on your file for six years.
  • Don't max out your card, even if you pay it off later.
  • Be careful with "buy now, pay later". It's now increasingly reported to credit agencies.

Check your file for free

You can check your credit file free through services linked to each agency. Look out for errors, like wrong addresses or accounts that aren't yours, and get them corrected.

Be patient

Credit is built over time. Do the basics consistently, and within a year you'll be in a much stronger position.

General information, not financial advice. MoneyHelper, backed by the UK government, offers free guidance.

posts.title: The japa checklist: 15 things to sort out before you leave Nigeria
posts.excerpt: Documents, money, phone, health and family. This is the checklist we wish someone had given us before our flight.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Before you japa, sort your documents (originals plus certified copies), keep your Nigerian bank accounts, BVN and NIN active, get transcripts and references, arrange how money will move, do a full health and dental check, and leave clear plans for family and property. Things that take five minutes in Lagos can take five months from abroad.

You've got your visa. Congratulations! 🎉 Now comes the part people underestimate: preparing to leave properly. Here's the checklist.

Documents

  1. Passport with plenty of validity. Renewing from abroad is possible but slower. If your passport expires within the next couple of years, consider renewing before you go.
  2. Certified copies of everything: birth certificate, degree certificates, transcripts, marriage certificate, children's birth certificates and any change-of-name documents. Scan them all to secure cloud storage too.
  3. Academic transcripts sent officially. If you'll need them for jobs or further study abroad, request them now. Universities can be very slow.
  4. Professional registrations and references. Nurses, doctors, engineers and teachers: get letters of good standing and work references while your old bosses still remember you.
  5. Driving history. Some countries take your Nigerian driving history into account for insurance. Get a letter from FRSC or keep your licence records.

Money

  1. Keep your Nigerian accounts active. Don't close them. Update your phone number and make sure internet banking works from abroad.
  2. Link your BVN and NIN and make sure the details match your passport exactly. Mismatched names cause endless problems.
  3. Arrange how money will move. Decide how you'll send money home and who will handle payments at home.
  4. Bring proof of funds and bank statements for your first weeks. Landlords and banks abroad may ask.

Phone and digital life

  1. Keep your Nigerian SIM active. Many banks still send OTPs by SMS. Set up a roaming plan or ask a trusted person to keep the SIM in a phone at home.
  2. Turn on two-factor authentication on email and social media using an authenticator app, not just SMS.

Health

  1. Full medical, dental and eye check. Dental work and glasses can cost much more abroad, and you may wait for appointments.
  2. Bring a record of your vaccinations and any prescriptions, plus a short supply of regular medication. Check the destination's rules for bringing medicines.

Family and property

  1. Leave clear instructions. If you own land or property, appoint someone you trust, ideally with a proper legal power of attorney. Many diaspora Nigerians have lost land to "family arrangements".
  2. Have the honest money conversation. Agree with family what support you can realistically send, especially in your first six months when costs are highest and income may not have started.

Bonus: the first-week bag

Pack your first week as if your suitcase gets lost: documents, chargers, a change of clothes, medication and a warm layer in your hand luggage.

Did we miss anything? Add your tip in the comments for the next person japa-ing.

posts.title: How to land your first UK job: CV tips every Nigerian professional should know
posts.excerpt: A CV that works in Lagos can get ignored in London. Here's how to rewrite yours for UK employers and get past the first screening.
posts.content:
Quick gist: UK CVs are two pages, with no photo, no date of birth, no marital status and no religion. Lead with a short profile, then show achievements with numbers. Tailor your CV for every job. If you need sponsorship, target employers on the government's sponsor register and say clearly what your right to work is.

Many skilled Nigerians arrive in the UK with great experience and still get silence from employers. Often the problem isn't you, it's your CV format. Here's how to fix it.

1. Remove what UK employers don't want

A typical Nigerian CV often includes:

  • ❌ Passport photo
  • ❌ Date of birth or age
  • ❌ Marital status, number of children
  • ❌ State of origin, religion
  • ❌ "Referees available" with full contact details on page one

In the UK, employers don't ask for these, partly because of equality and anti-discrimination rules. Including them can make your CV look out of place. Remove them.

2. Keep it to two pages

UK recruiters skim. Two pages is standard for most roles. Put the most recent and relevant experience first.

3. Start with a sharp profile

Three or four lines at the top that say who you are, what you do and what you're looking for:

Chartered accountant with 7 years' experience in audit and financial reporting across banking and telecoms. ACCA-qualified, skilled in IFRS and SAP. Seeking a financial reporting role in the NHS or public sector.

4. Achievements, not duties

Compare these:

  • ❌ "Responsible for managing the sales team."
  • ✅ "Led a team of 8 to grow regional sales by 32% in 12 months."

Use numbers wherever possible: money saved, targets hit, people managed, processes improved.

5. Translate your experience

UK employers may not know Nigerian companies or qualifications. Add context:

  • "Dangote Group (one of Africa's largest industrial conglomerates)"
  • If useful, get your qualifications compared through the UK's official recognition service (UK ENIC) and mention it.

6. Tailor it for every application

Read the job advert and use its key words in your CV, especially the skills listed under "essential criteria". Many employers use software to screen CVs before a human sees them.

7. Be clear about your right to work

  • If you have the right to work (for example, a Graduate visa, dependant visa or ILR), say so briefly: "Full right to work in the UK (Graduate visa, valid to 2028)."
  • If you need sponsorship, target employers on the GOV.UK register of licensed sponsors. It lists every organisation that can sponsor Skilled Worker visas.

8. Write a short cover letter

For many jobs, especially in the public sector and NHS, the supporting statement matters as much as the CV. Address each essential criterion with a real example.

9. Use LinkedIn properly

Recruiters search LinkedIn constantly. Use a professional photo (yes, the photo goes on LinkedIn, not your CV), a clear headline and the same achievements as your CV.

Don't give up

Rejections are part of the process, even for people who were senior at home. Many Nigerians start a step lower and climb quickly once they have UK experience. Keep applying, keep improving and lean on your network.

Want a tool to check your visa costs while you job hunt? Try VisaCost Hub.

posts.title: Raising Naija kids abroad: how to keep the culture (and the language) alive
posts.excerpt: Your children may grow up with British, Canadian or American accents. Here's how to make sure they still know where they come from.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Speak your language at home every day, even if they reply in English. Make Nigerian food, music and stories normal rather than "special occasion". Connect them with grandparents by video regularly. Find community: church, cultural associations and Saturday schools. And when you can afford it, take them home.

One day your child will say "Mum, can we have pasta instead?" in a perfect British accent, and you'll realise the culture won't pass on by itself. Here's how many diaspora parents keep it alive.

1. Speak the language at home, consistently

This is the one most of us struggle with. It feels easier to switch to English, especially when they answer in English. But children pick up languages they hear daily, even if they don't speak them back at first.

  • Pick one language at home (Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Pidgin or another) and stick with it, at least at meals and bedtime.
  • Don't panic if they reply in English. Understanding comes first, and speaking follows.
  • Use songs, cartoons and YouTube channels in your language. There are more than ever.

UNESCO and many researchers note that children benefit from keeping their home language. It doesn't hold back their English.

2. Make Naija food everyday food

If jollof only appears at parties, it becomes "party food" rather than "our food". Cook Nigerian meals during the normal week. Let them help: washing beans, frying plantain, stirring the pot. Food is memory.

3. Grandparents on video, regularly

Weekly video calls with grandma and grandpa build a bond that can last a lifetime. Let the grandparents tell stories, sing the old songs and ask about school. Even if it's chaotic, it matters.

4. Find your community

  • Churches and mosques with large Nigerian congregations
  • Cultural associations, such as state or ethnic unions, often organised by town
  • Saturday schools that teach language, history and culture
  • Naija playdates with other diaspora families, so it's not just your weird mum doing it 😄

5. Teach them the stories

Tell them about your village, your school and what Christmas was like at home. Teach them proverbs and folk tales. Show them old family photos. Children are proud of what they understand.

6. Celebrate both identities

Your child can be fully British, Canadian or American and fully Nigerian. Avoid making them feel they have to choose. Celebrate Independence Day on 1 October and Bonfire Night, Thanksgiving or Canada Day too.

7. Take them home

Nothing beats the real thing. Even one trip every few years, to see the markets, hear the noise and eat agege bread from the roadside, can anchor their identity for life. Start saving early; it's worth it.

How are you keeping the culture alive in your home? Share your tips in the comments.

posts.title: Sending money home: 7 mistakes that cost Nigerians abroad thousands every year
posts.excerpt: From hidden fees to "black tax" burnout, these are the most common money-transfer mistakes, and how to fix each one.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Most people lose money on transfers through hidden exchange-rate margins, small frequent sends and no budget for family support. Compare the amount received, batch your transfers, agree a monthly figure with family, and keep records.

Supporting family back home is part of life for most of us abroad. But between fees, poor rates and endless "urgent" requests, a lot of hard-earned money leaks away. Here are the seven mistakes we see most, and how to fix them.

1. Comparing the rate, not the amount received

An app might show a shiny rate but charge a £3.99 fee, while another has no fee and a slightly weaker rate. The only number that matters is how much naira lands in the account for the pounds you put in. Always compare that.

2. Sending small amounts many times

Fixed fees eat small transfers alive. Sending £30 four times a month can cost several times more in fees than sending £120 once. Where you can, batch your sends.

3. Using your bank's international transfer

High-street banks often charge a flat fee plus a poor exchange rate. For most people, a specialist transfer service is much cheaper. The World Bank tracks remittance costs worldwide, and banks are consistently among the most expensive channels.

4. No monthly "family support" budget

If every request is treated as a surprise, you'll never know how much you actually send. Sit down once and set a fixed monthly figure for family support. Share it with whoever coordinates at home. It's kinder for everyone than yes-no-yes-no every week.

5. Sending to the wrong account in a rush

Mistyped account numbers, especially with similar bank names, are common and painful to reverse. Save trusted recipients in your app and double-check new ones. Never send to a new account just because a WhatsApp message asked you to. Call the person first, because family accounts get hacked too.

6. Ignoring the rules

Since May 2026, licensed transfer companies pay out in naira at market rates. Using unlicensed dealers or random crypto traders to "beat the rate" can leave your family's account frozen. The few naira you save aren't worth it.

7. Paying "black tax" with no plan for yourself

Supporting family is honourable, but not at the expense of your rent, emergency fund and pension. Financial advisers often suggest building three months of expenses as an emergency fund first. A broke you can't help anyone next year.

A simple system that works

  1. Pick one main transfer app and one backup.
  2. Set a monthly family amount and send it on the same day each month.
  3. Keep a small "emergency home fund" in a separate pot for genuine emergencies.
  4. Keep records of what you sent and why.

You'll send the same love with a lot less stress.

General information, not financial advice.
